steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a quality indicator that measures the spread of a set of software architecture design alternatives in the architectural space instead of the objective space. Cover the multi-objective refactoring setting, quality indicators such as maximum spread, and what we propose.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Automated generation of architecture design alternatives through refactoring; multi-objective setting
2. Configuring multi-objective optimization; quality indicators and maximum spread
3. Why spread matters for architectures; limits of objective-space indicators
4. Our proposal (MAS) and preliminary results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Context
- designing/evolving software architectures: improving quality attributes (performance, reliability, maintainability) = central concern
- increasing number of automated approaches generating improved versions of an initial architecture
- generated architectures = design alternatives; produced through refactoring (transformations improving quality attributes, functionalities unchanged)
- designer tackles multiple attributes at once, e.g. improve performance, keep reliability high, refactoring cost low -> multi-objective optimization

2. Quality indicators
- multi-objective optimization needs experiments to set configuration parameters (choice of algorithm + settings, e.g. specific genetic algorithm, population size)
- recurring problem: which configuration to prefer given obtained solution sets
- traditionally: quality indicators for solution sets; estimate desirable properties, help choose parameters
- spread: how much of solution space covered, how diverse solutions are
- maximum spread (MS): prominent indicator; higher MS = search covered a wide area

3. Spread for architectures
- especially relevant: sizeable number of alternatives found; tradeoffs dispersed -> variety of design choices
- indicators computed on problem objectives (performance, reliability, cost in example)
- good for assessing optimization algorithms, but no insight into architectural features of solutions (architectural space), closer to the actual SE task

4. Proposal
- MAS (Maximum Architecture Spread): architectural quality indicator for spread in sets of design alternatives
- based on maximum spread, but architectural space instead of objective space
- demo on dataset from an architecture optimization problem in the literature
- differences among alternatives based on structure: encode architectures as sequences of refactorings, distance metrics on encodings
- preliminary results: additional architectural view of optimization; correlation with MS

A prominent indicator for this property is the maximum spread (MS). If MS is higher, it means the optimization searched the solution space enough to cover a wide area.

- especially relevant: sizeable number of alternatives found; tradeoffs dispersed -> variety of design choices
- indicators computed on problem objectives (performance, reliability, cost in example)
- good for assessing optimization algorithms, but no insight into architectural features of solutions (architectural space), closer to the actual SE task

- \mathit{MAS} (Maximum Architecture Spread): architectural quality indicator for spread in sets of design alternatives

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When software architectures are designed or evolved, the designer is mainly concerned with improving quality attributes such as performance, reliability or maintainability. Recently there has been an increasing number of automated approaches that target this task, and their goal is to generate improved versions of an initial architecture. The architectures they generate are called design alternatives. The alternatives are generated automatically through refactoring, which means applying transformations that improve some quality attributes of interest while the software functionalities stay the same. In practice the designer deals with multiple attributes at the same time. For example she might want to improve performance but also keep reliability high and keep the cost of refactoring low. This kind of context is ideal for multi-objective optimization.

Multi-objective optimization usually needs a series of experiments to find good configuration parameters. These parameters can be for example the choice of the optimization algorithm and its settings, like which genetic algorithm is used and its population size. A problem that comes up again and again is deciding which configuration parameters should be preferred based on the solution sets that were obtained. In multi-objective optimization this has traditionally been handled with quality indicators for solution sets. The indicators try to estimate desirable properties of the solution sets, so they can help designers choose parameters that improve those properties. One of these properties is the spread of a solution set, which plays a fundamental role in assessing how much of the solution space was covered and how diverse the solutions in the set are. A prominent indicator for this property is the maximum spread (MS). If MS is higher, it means the optimization searched the solution space enough to cover a wide area.

Spread is especially relevant when we deal with architectural alternatives. It shows that a sizeable number of alternatives were found, and that the solution set covers tradeoffs that are dispersed enough to give the designer a variety of design choices. However, quality indicators are computed on the problem objectives, i.e. the attributes being optimized (performance, reliability, and cost in the example above). These indicators are valuable to assess the performance of optimization algorithms, but they do not give insights on the architectural features of the solutions, i.e., the architectural space, and it is the architectural space that represents more closely the object of the software engineering task we described.

In this paper we propose an architectural quality indicator called \mathit{MAS} (Maximum Architecture Spread) to estimate the spread in sets of design alternatives. \mathit{MAS} is based on the notion of maximum spread from prior work, but it works in the architectural space instead of the objective space. To show our approach, we apply \mathit{MAS} to a dataset that addresses an architecture optimization problem from the literature. For this we calculate the differences among architectural alternatives based on their structure. We do this by first encoding the architectures as sequences of refactorings and then using distance metrics on these encodings. Our preliminary results show that MAS gives an additional architectural view of the optimization, and that it is correlated with the (MS) indicator.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
When designing or evolving software architectures, the improvement of quality attributes like performance, reliability, or maintainability is a central concern for the designer. This task has recently been targeted by an increasing number of automated approaches whose goal is to generate improved versions of an initial architecture [1,2]. The generated architectures are called design alternatives. These alternatives are automatically generated through refactoring, i.e., the application of transformations that improve some quality attributes of interest while keeping the software functionalities unchanged. In practical cases, the designer tackles multiple attributes at the same time. For example, she could aim at improving performance while keeping reliability high and the cost of refactoring low. This context is ideal for multi-objective optimization.

Multi-objective optimization normally needs a series of experiments to determine appropriate configuration parameters, such as the choice of the optimization algorithm and its settings (e.g., the specific genetic algorithm and its population size). A recurring problem is deciding which configuration parameters should be preferred on the basis of the obtained solution sets. In multi-objective optimization, this issue has traditionally been addressed by means of quality indicators for solution sets [3]. These indicators estimate desirable properties of solution sets and can therefore help designers choose parameters that improve such properties. Among these properties, the spread of a solution set plays a fundamental role in assessing how much of the solution space was covered and how diverse the solutions in the set are. The maximum spread (MS) [4] is a prominent indicator for this property. Higher MS values indicate that the optimization searched the solution space enough to cover a wide area.

The spread is especially relevant when dealing with architectural alternatives. It shows that a sizeable number of alternatives were found, and that the obtained solution set covers tradeoffs dispersed enough to provide the designer with a variety of design choices. Note that quality indicators are computed on the problem objectives, i.e., the attributes being optimized (performance, reliability, and cost in the previous example). Although these indicators are valuable for assessing the performance of optimization algorithms, they give no insights on the architectural features of the solutions, i.e., the architectural space, which more closely represents the object of the software engineering task we described.

In this paper, we propose an architectural quality indicator, called \mathit{MAS} (Maximum Architecture Spread), for estimating the spread in sets of design alternatives. \mathit{MAS} is based on the notion of maximum spread by [4], but it operates in the architectural space instead of the objective space. To demonstrate our approach, we show how \mathit{MAS} can be applied to a dataset that addresses an architecture optimization problem from the literature. To do this, we calculate the differences among architectural alternatives based on their structure, by first encoding the architectures as sequences of refactorings and then using distance metrics on such encodings. Our preliminary results indicate that MAS provides an additional architectural view of the optimization and exhibits a correlation with the (MS) indicator.

References:
[1] Cortellessa, V., Di Pompeo, D., Stoico, V., Tucci, M.: Many-objective optimization of non-functional attributes based on refactoring of software models. Information and Software Technology 157 , 107159 (2023)
[2] Ni, Y., Du, X., Ye, P., Minku, L.L., Yao, X., Harman, M., Xiao, R.: Multi-objective software performance optimisation at the architecture level using randomised search rules. Information and Software Technology 135 , 106565 (2021)
[3] Li, M., Yao, X.: Quality evaluation of solution sets in multiobjective optimisation: A survey. ACM Comput. Surv. 52 (2), 26:1–26:38 (2019)
[4] Zitzler, E., Deb, K., Thiele, L.: Comparison of multiobjective evolutionary algorithms: Empirical results. Evol. Comput. 8 (2), 173–195 (2000)
